description: Hamilton was created to build a bridge between actual NASA operations and young people who dream of exploring space. Through interactive simulations that cover everything from planning to execution, we reveal what goes on behind the scenes of a space mission—going well beyond the iconic "Moon landing" by demonstrating, in practical terms, every decision that ensures the crew's safety. Our goal is to spark curiosity and foster learning about real space missions, bringing space to you.
summary:
Hamilton's Mission: A Space Adventure is a 16-bit retro web game inspired by software engineering pioneer Margaret Hamilton. Designed to run instantly in any browser with zero external dependencies, it puts players in command of a Lunar Research Station and an Autonomous Mars Habitat.
To address the challenge of translating complex space science into engaging education, the game integrates real NASA open data—including DONKI space weather alerts, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) irradiance and thermal datasets, and Mars Perseverance and Curiosity telemetry. Each turn, authentic environmental hazards drain station reserves, forcing players to inspect server terminals, analyze live telemetry curves, and make tough engineering trade-offs across Energy, Life Support, and Shielding while managing delayed cascade effects and Earth-to-Mars communication delay.

This project is important because real spaceflight rarely offers risk-free solutions. By turning raw telemetry into interactive systems-engineering decisions, it builds critical thinking in young explorers and connects them directly to real-world NASA Citizen Science initiatives like GLOBE Observer, Sungrazer, Aurorasaurus, and AI4Mars.
details:
WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS

Hamilton's Mission: A Space Adventure is an interactive, browser-based 16-bit retro simulation game that puts players in command of a Lunar Research Station (Mode 1) and an Autonomous Mars Habitat (Mode 2). Guided by APOLLO, an onboard AI copilot, players manage three coupled station subsystems: Energy, Life Support, and Shielding. Each phase spans three turns (or Sols on Mars) driven by real NASA space weather, lunar, and Martian telemetry. Every turn, an environmental hazard drains station reserves. Players walk across the station floor to inspect three interactive server terminals—Power Reactor, Bio-Dome Life Support, and Defense & Telemetry—where they view a real-time NASA sensor curve chart, compare protocol options, and preview exact net resource math before committing. Because every protocol involves a trade-off (such as boosting shielding at the cost of battery power or triggering a delayed cascade effect on the next turn) and reserves carry over between phases, letting any bar reach 0% triggers station collapse and restarts the campaign.

In Mode 1, players navigate three historic crises inspired by Apollo 13 power rationing, Skylab thermal overload, and the August 1972 solar storm.

Unlocking Mode 2 transitions the commander into an EVA space suit on Mars, where players select a landing zone (Jezero Crater or Elysium Planitia) that modifies starting reserves. Simulating the real Earth-to-Mars radio signal delay, APOLLO disables guided hints and switches to Autonomous Mode, challenging players to interpret raw MEDA dust, RAD radiation, and MOXIE oxygen values independently. To assist evaluators, a "JUDGE PASS" toggle in the top bar unlocks Mode 2 immediately.

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT

Instead of passive memorization, the game teaches systems engineering, critical thinking, and data literacy through cause-and-effect experimentation. Players immediately see how real orbital and planetary telemetry governs crew survival. Upon completing the campaign, players receive a performance rank (up to Flight Director Distinction), generate a personalized downloadable PNG Mars Commander Certificate, and unlock direct links to real NASA Citizen Science projects—GLOBE Observer, Sungrazer, Aurorasaurus, and AI4Mars—turning gameplay into active scientific participation.

TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE & SOFTWARE USED

- Languages & Web Standards: Vanilla HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+) with zero external frameworks or heavy dependencies.

- Graphics & Visualization: Custom HTML5 Canvas 2D pixel-art rendering engine, SVG pixel icons, real-time telemetry curve plotter, and an automated PNG certificate generator.

- Procedural Audio: Custom Web Audio API 8-bit synthesizer generating sound effects and space-opera background music mathematically in the browser without external MP3 files.

- Data Integration: Asynchronous fetch integration with the live NASA DONKI Space Weather API paired with a structured JSON mission archive fallback.

- Development & Deployment: Built on standard laptops using VS Code, Git, and GitHub, and deployed publicly via GitHub Pages.

CREATIVITY & DESIGN FACTORS CONSIDERED

- Historical & STEM Inspiration: Named in honor of Margaret Hamilton, whose Apollo flight software prioritized critical tasks under resource constraints—the core mechanic of our game.

- Accessibility & Equity: Built with zero-install browser execution and lightweight procedural assets so students on low-spec school computers or slow connections can play instantly, with full English/Portuguese toggling to broaden STEM inclusion.

- Pedagogical Clarity: We designed segmented resource bars with damage trails and pre-decision net-outcome previews so younger players can grasp trade-offs visually rather than guessing blindly.
